topic: The fight dominating the weekend of July 25-26, 2026 is President Trump's replacement tariff regime: at 12:01 a.m. ET on Friday, July 24 — the hour the 150-day Section 122 global tariff expired by operation of law — new duties of 10% to 12.5% took effect on goods from 60 economies covering roughly 99.4% of U.S. imports, imposed not as an emergency measure but under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 on the theory that each of those 60 economies commits an 'unreasonable' act by failing to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on importing goods made with forced labor. It is the third legal theory the administration has used for essentially the same across-the-board tariff wall in eighteen months: IEEPA tariffs (struck down 6-3 by the Supreme Court on February 20, 2026), then a temporary 10% Section 122 balance-of-payments surcharge, and now Section 301 — plus a separate 25% Section 301 action against Brazil effective July 22 and open 'excess capacity' Section 301 investigations aimed at another sixteen economies. By the weekend two sets of small importers — including Learning Resources, the plaintiff that beat the administration at the Supreme Court in February, and the spice company Burlap and Barrel — had sued at the U.S. Court of International Trade, arguing Section 301 'is not a freestanding authorization to tax substantially all imports from substantially all trading partners.' Trading partners from Australia to Brazil to New Zealand rejected the forced-labor rationale; the European Commission, by contrast, welcomed the outcome as 'in line with the agreed tariff commitments' of its trade deal. The checkable core: the statute's text and what it requires, whether the tariff rates track forced-labor conduct or trade-deal status, who pays, and whether this survives judicial review.
question: On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative imposed additional duties of 10%-12.5% on 60 economies — about 99.4% of U.S. imports — under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, finding that each economy's failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced-labor import prohibition is 'unreasonable' and 'burdens or restricts U.S. commerce.' Defenders answer that forced labor in global supply chains is real and documented, that the United States has banned forced-labor imports since the Tariff Act of 1930 while almost no one else does, that USTR ran a four-month statutory investigation with hearings and thousands of comments, and that Section 301 is exactly the tool Congress wrote for unfair foreign practices — as Ambassador Greer put it, 'it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same.' Critics — Democratic officeholders and attorneys general, most trade economists, the importers now suing, and much of the free-trade right — answer that the timing (to the hour of Section 122's expiry), the rate structure (which tracks who signed a trade deal, not who tolerates forced labor), and the absence of any compliance benchmark show a revenue-and-leverage program with a human-rights label, imposed under a statute Congress never wrote to tax nearly all imports from nearly all countries. Which side's checkable claims hold up?
summary:
The most-argued political story of the July 25-26, 2026 weekend is the new Section 301 'forced labor' tariff wall that took effect Friday and the lawsuits filed against it within hours. The day leans left — that is, toward the tariffs' critics — but only moderately, because the administration's central factual predicate is true and inconvenient for its opponents, and because the legal question at the heart of the fight is genuinely open rather than settled.

What holds up on the administration's side, verified in primary documents: the United States really has prohibited forced-labor imports since 1930 (19 U.S.C. § 1307: such goods 'shall not be entitled to entry at any of the ports of the United States'), and most of its trading partners really do not have — or do not enforce — an equivalent import ban. USTR's own Federal Register notice determines that 54 of the 60 investigated economies 'have failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor' and six more (Canada, Ecuador, the EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan) have failed to enforce one. That asymmetry is real, it is a longstanding complaint of American manufacturers and unions, and the praise USTR collected came not only from Republicans but from the United Steelworkers and the Machinists. USTR also ran a real statutory process: investigations initiated March 12, 2026, hearings in April and July, thousands of comments, an exemption list expanded after comment.

What does not hold up is the claim that this particular tariff schedule is calibrated to forced labor. The tariffs took effect at 12:01 a.m. on the exact day the temporary Section 122 surcharge expired, at essentially the level it had been. The rate split is set — by USTR's own words — by whether an economy has an import prohibition, 'a partial regime,' or 'commitments related to forced labor import prohibitions through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade.' The practical result is an inversion: Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka pay the lower 10% rate, while Australia, New Zealand and Norway pay the higher 12.5%. The European Commission's own reaction is the cleanest receipt against the human-rights framing — Brussels welcomed the outcome as 'in line with the agreed tariff commitments' of the trade deal it struck last year. And USTR's own summary of the strategy, as reported the week of the action, was that 'the specific authorities this administration is using have changed, but the trade strategy has not.'

The legal question is unresolved and both sides overclaim about it. Section 301's own text enumerates a worker-rights category of 'unreasonable' conduct — a 'persistent pattern of conduct that ... permits any form of forced or compulsory labor' — but that clause comes with a statutory safe harbor: such practices 'shall not be treated as being unreasonable' if USTR finds them 'not inconsistent with the level of economic development of the foreign country.' USTR did not rest on that enumerated clause; it rested on the open-ended chapeau ('include, but are not limited to') and a novel theory that failing to police *other countries'* forced-labor goods burdens U.S. commerce. Congress's own research service, writing three days before the action, flagged the vulnerabilities without predicting an outcome: actionability, the major-questions doctrine, and APA 'arbitrary, capricious' review of what critics call cursory country-by-country findings. Trade lawyers are split on whether these tariffs are more or less durable than the IEEPA ones. Anyone telling you the courts will certainly strike them — or certainly uphold them — is guessing.

What the meter cannot decide: whether tariffs are a legitimate tool of human-rights policy at all, whether the trade-off between higher consumer prices and domestic manufacturing employment is worth it, whether Congress should claw back the tariff delegations it has made, and whether pressuring poorer countries to adopt import bans is help or imposition. Those are value questions and they are listed where they belong.
verdict: On the checkable present-tense facts this leans toward the tariffs' critics, and not by a landslide. The administration's core factual predicate survives scrutiny: the U.S. forced-labor import ban dates to the Tariff Act of 1930, most trading partners lack or do not enforce an equivalent, and USTR's determination to that effect rests on a four-month investigation with hearings and thousands of comments — a process the critics mostly talk past rather than rebut. What fails is the calibration claim. The duties took effect at 12:01 a.m. on the very day the temporary Section 122 surcharge lapsed, at roughly the same level; the rate split turns on trade-deal commitments and partial regimes rather than measured forced-labor conduct, producing the inversion in which Bangladesh, Cambodia, India and Pakistan pay 10% while Australia, New Zealand and Norway pay 12.5%; and the European Commission publicly welcomed the result as 'in line with the agreed tariff commitments' of its trade deal — an odd thing to say about a human-rights sanction. On the law, both sides overclaim. Section 301's enumerated worker-rights clause covers a country's own 'persistent pattern of conduct that ... permits any form of forced or compulsory labor' and carries a safe harbor for practices 'not inconsistent with the level of economic development of the foreign country'; USTR avoided that clause and built a non-enumerated theory on the statute's open-ended chapeau. Whether that survives is an open question Congress's own research service framed as genuinely uncertain, and trade lawyers split on it — so 'these tariffs are plainly illegal' is a prediction, not a fact, and the critics who assert it are doing what they accuse the administration of doing. What the meter does not decide: whether tariffs are an appropriate instrument of human-rights policy, whether higher import prices are worth whatever domestic production they buy, or whether Congress should reclaim the delegations that made any of this possible.

left.label: They lost at the Supreme Court in February, so they went shopping for a new statute. The emergency-powers tariffs were struck down 6-3; the temporary balance-of-payments surcharge ran out its 150 days at midnight Thursday; and at 12:01 a.m. Friday the same tariff wall reappeared wearing a human-rights badge. If this were really about forced labor, the rates would track forced labor. They don't. Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka pay 10 percent. Australia, New Zealand and Norway pay 12.5 percent. The thing that determines your rate is not whether your workers are coerced — it's whether your government signed one of the president's trade deals, which is why Brussels put out a statement *welcoming* the tariffs as consistent with the bargain it struck. USTR's own trade representative summed it up: the authorities changed, the strategy didn't. Congress wrote Section 301 to answer specific unfair practices by specific countries, not to hand a president a permanent 12.5 percent tax on 99.4 percent of everything Americans import, collected from American importers and paid by American households. And there is no benchmark any country can meet to get out from under it — which is how you know what it's for.
left.framing: The critics' checkable claims are unusually tight: the timing, the rate structure, the EU's own reception, USTR's own statement of continuity, the coverage figure, and the fact that tariffs are collected from U.S. importers are all documented, several of them from the administration's own paper. This coalition is also broader than the left — Cato and the free-trade right make the pretext argument more sharply than most Democrats do, which is the strongest possible corroboration. The honest version concedes three things the meter credits to the other side: forced labor in supply chains is real and the U.S. import ban is genuinely near-unique; most of the 60 economies genuinely do lack an enforced import prohibition; and USTR genuinely ran the statutory process, with hearings, thousands of comments and an expanded exemption list. The weakest move available to this side is to assert the courts will strike the tariffs down — a prediction on an open question, contradicted by trade lawyers who think Section 301 is sturdier ground than IEEPA — and to argue as though the forced-labor problem were invented for the occasion.
left.strongestPoint: The calibration test, which the administration's own documents fail. USTR's Federal Register notice states the criterion for the lower rate in its own words: economies that impose a prohibition, 'have taken on commitments related to forced labor import prohibitions through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade,' or 'have imposed a partial regime.' Run that criterion against the published lists and you get Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka at 10% while Australia, New Zealand and Norway sit at 12.5% — the rate rises as measured forced-labor risk falls. The European Commission then supplied the receipt no critic could have written for them, welcoming the outcome as 'in line with the agreed tariff commitments' of its trade deal. Add the timing — 12:01 a.m. on the exact day the Section 122 surcharge expired by operation of law, at essentially the same level — and the administration's own trade representative's line that 'the specific authorities this administration is using have changed, but the trade strategy has not,' and the pretext case is made out of primary material rather than inference.
left.weakestPoint: This side keeps predicting judicial outcomes it cannot know and treating the underlying grievance as fictitious. Congress's own research service, writing three days before the action, laid out the vulnerabilities — actionability, major questions, APA review — without predicting a result, and trade lawyers quoted in the same coverage think Section 301 is harder to beat than IEEPA precisely because it comes with a real investigative record and deferential substantial-evidence review. 'Unlikely to survive court' is a forecast dressed as a finding. Worse, much of the criticism never engages the factual predicate: 54 economies really have no forced-labor import ban, the U.S. really has had one since 1930, and the United Steelworkers and the Machinists — not natural allies of this administration — publicly backed the action. A critique that cannot say out loud what is true in the other side's case is doing advocacy, not analysis.
left.unknowns: Whether the Court of International Trade or the Federal Circuit will find the failure to impose an import prohibition 'actionable' under Section 301 is unknown and will not be known for months. Whether the tariffs will in fact induce any country to adopt an import ban — the statutory purpose — cannot be assessed a weekend after they took effect. The share of the 60 economies' exports to the U.S. actually tainted by forced labor is not established in the public record, and Cato's estimate of a proportionate 0.23-1% rate is its own calculation, not an independently verified figure.

right.label: America banned forced-labor imports in 1930 and has enforced that ban for nearly a century. Almost nobody else does. The result is that goods made by coerced workers get shut out of one market and dumped into everyone else's — and American workers compete against that price. USTR opened sixty investigations in March, held hearings in April and July, took more than two thousand comments, consulted forty-five governments, and found what anyone honest already knew: fifty-four of these economies have no forced-labor import prohibition at all, and six more don't enforce the one they have. That is the definition of an unreasonable practice that burdens American commerce, and Section 301 is the statute Congress wrote for exactly that. Ten to twelve and a half percent, with raw materials and critical supply chains carved out and textile quotas offered to countries willing to move — that is a modest, targeted instrument, and countries can get relief by acting. The Steelworkers back it. The Machinists back it. The steel industry backs it. The people screaming loudest are importers who profit from the status quo and foreign governments that would rather lecture America about human rights than police their own docks.
right.framing: The defenders' verified strengths are real and are the reason this day is not a rout: the 1930 statute exists and says what they say it says; the near-uniqueness of the U.S. import ban is confirmed in USTR's own country-by-country determinations and disputed by no trading partner on the merits of the gap itself; the statutory process was genuinely run rather than skipped; the exemption list was expanded after comment; and the coalition includes unions whose endorsement cannot be dismissed as partisan. The case collapses on the join between the grievance and this remedy. Nothing in the record explains why the rate schedule tracks trade-deal status rather than forced-labor conduct, why the duties began at the precise hour a different tariff authority lapsed at nearly the same level, why the human-rights measure is one the European Commission publicly welcomed as consistent with its trade bargain, or why there is no published benchmark by which a country can earn removal. And 'the trade strategy has not changed' is the administration's own sentence, not a critic's characterization.
right.strongestPoint: The factual predicate is true and is the part critics keep stepping around. 19 U.S.C. § 1307, enacted as § 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930, provides that goods made 'wholly or in part in any foreign country by convict labor or/and forced labor or/and indentured labor under penal sanctions ... shall not be entitled to entry at any of the ports of the United States.' Almost no trading partner has an equivalent enforced prohibition, and USTR's determinations name them one by one — 54 that have failed to impose and effectively enforce such a ban, six more that have failed to enforce one. The asymmetry has a real economic consequence that Section 301 is at least plausibly addressed to: goods excluded from the U.S. market flow elsewhere, and producers who refuse forced-labor inputs compete on a tilted field. This is also the rare trade action endorsed by the United Steelworkers and the Machinists as well as by the House Ways and Means chairman — a cross-partisan coalition on the merits of the grievance, whatever one thinks of the remedy.
right.weakestPoint: Everything about the instrument contradicts the stated purpose. The lower 10% rate goes, by USTR's own published criterion, to economies with 'commitments ... through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade' — so Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka pay less than Australia, New Zealand and Norway. The measure took effect at 12:01 a.m. on the day the Section 122 surcharge expired, replacing a 10% global tariff with a 10-12.5% global tariff covering 99.4% of imports. The European Commission welcomed it as 'in line with the agreed tariff commitments' — a sentence no genuine human-rights sanction earns from its target. USTR itself said the authorities changed but the strategy did not. And on the law, the administration deliberately avoided Section 301's one enumerated forced-labor clause, which would have triggered the statutory safe harbor for practices 'not inconsistent with the level of economic development of the foreign country,' in favor of an unenumerated theory that a country's failure to police third-country goods burdens U.S. commerce — a theory Congress's own research service flags as untested and vulnerable to major-questions and arbitrary-and-capricious review.
right.unknowns: Whether the rate structure was in fact set by trade-deal status rather than forced-labor findings cannot be proven from the public record; USTR's incorporated report is asserted to support each determination, and its country-by-country reasoning has not been independently audited here. Whether any of the 60 economies will now adopt or enforce an import prohibition is unknown. Whether the courts will treat the four-month investigative record as substantial evidence, or as the 'cursory' findings critics describe, is genuinely open. And whether tariff revenue or forced labor was the operative motive is a question about intent that the documents alone cannot settle.

facts.claim: USTR determined that 54 of 60 investigated economies have failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on importing goods made with forced labor, and six more (Canada, Ecuador, the EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan) have failed to enforce one — and the United States has had such an import ban since 1930.
facts.evidence: USTR Federal Register notice (primary, text extracted directly): 'The following 54 economies have failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; ... New Zealand; ... Norway; ...' and 'The following six economies have failed to effectively enforce a prohibition' — Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan. 19 U.S.C. § 1307 (Tariff Act of 1930 § 307, read directly): goods made 'by convict labor or/and forced labor or/and indentured labor under penal sanctions shall not be entitled to entry at any of the ports of the United States, and the importation thereof is hereby prohibited.'
facts.explanation: This is the administration's strongest ground and it holds. The 1930 statute says what Ambassador Greer said it says ('a forced labor import ban for nearly a century'), and no trading partner disputed the underlying gap on the merits — Canada answered that it maintains 'robust frameworks,' and the EU adopted its own forced-labour products regulation only in December 2024, with member states not required even to designate enforcement authorities until December 2025. The honest caveat is that a 'failure to impose an import prohibition' is a legal-architecture finding, not a measurement of forced labor: an economy can appear on the 54-country list while having low forced-labor prevalence, and USTR's incorporated country-by-country report has been criticized (by Cato) as running roughly half a page per country. The determination that the gap exists is well supported; the determination that the gap is 'unreasonable' within the meaning of the statute is a separate question graded below.

facts.evidence: USTR Federal Register notice (primary, read directly): 'For economies that impose a forced labor import prohibition; have taken on commitments related to forced labor import prohibitions through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade; or have imposed a partial regime ... the Trade Representative proposes 10% as the rate of additional duties. For all other economies, the Trade Representative proposes 12.5%.' USTR press release of July 23, 2026 (read directly) lists the 10% group: 'Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, United Kingdom.' Australia, New Zealand and Norway appear on the 54-economy 'failed to impose' list and are not in the 10% group.
facts.explanation: The inversion is verifiable from two primary documents read directly: the criterion for the lower rate and the list of who received it. Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka — economies that feature heavily in international forced-labor risk assessments and in the U.S. government's own supply-chain concerns — sit in the 10% tier, while Australia, New Zealand and Norway sit at 12.5%. The administration's defense is available and should be stated: the criterion is not forced-labor prevalence but whether an economy has an import prohibition, a partial regime, or has made commitments in a trade agreement, so a country that promised action in a bilateral deal earns the discount regardless of its starting point. That is internally coherent as an incentive design. What it is not is a schedule calibrated to forced-labor conduct — which is the specific claim critics make and the specific claim that holds. CRS independently flagged that rates 'may have tied ... to diplomatic considerations rather than forced labor practices alone.'
facts.source: USTR — 'USTR Takes Action in Forced Labor Section 301 Investigations' (July 23, 2026)

corroboration.source: The White House — Presidential memorandum, Actions under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 (July 23, 2026)
CRS — Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs to Address Forced Labor and Excess Manufacturing Capacity (LSB11460, July 21, 2026)

facts.claim: The new tariffs took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on July 24, 2026 — the moment the temporary 10% Section 122 global surcharge expired by operation of law — and cover roughly 99.4% of U.S. imports at 10%-12.5%.
facts.evidence: EY Tax News (read directly): additional duties 'take effect 24 July 2026' at 12:01 a.m. ET under new HTS subheadings 9903.05.20 through 9903.05.84, replacing the expiring Section 122 tariffs. Grant Thornton (read directly): new tariffs 'took effect on July 24, 2026 at 12:01 a.m., replacing a 10% global duty that expired simultaneously,' with Greer quoted: 'The specific authorities this administration is using have changed, but the trade strategy has not.' Supply Chain Dive (read directly): the tariffs 'apply to approximately 99.4% of U.S. imports.'
facts.explanation: The seamlessness is the point both sides argue about, and it is not in dispute as a fact: Section 122 of the Trade Act caps a balance-of-payments surcharge at 15% for 150 days and cannot be extended unilaterally, so the 10% global tariff imposed hours after the February 20 Supreme Court ruling lapsed on July 24, and the Section 301 duties began the same instant at 10-12.5%. One source conflict is surfaced rather than smoothed: an Associated Press account reprinted July 26-27 dates the effect to July 26, while USTR's notice, EY, Grant Thornton and Supply Chain Dive all give July 24; the primary documents are followed here. The 99.4% coverage figure appears in trade-press reporting and is consistent with PIIE's independent description of the 60 economies as 'nearly all US imports and 90 percent of world trade.'
facts.source: Grant Thornton — New tariffs imposed on countries as Section 122 expires

corroboration.source: EY Tax News — USTR finalizes Section 301 forced labor tariffs on 60 economies
Supply Chain Dive — US imposes tariffs over forced labor before global duty ends

facts.claim: Section 301's text enumerates a worker-rights category of 'unreasonable' conduct covering a country that permits forced labor — but with a safe harbor for practices 'not inconsistent with the level of economic development of the foreign country' — and USTR did not rest its determination on that clause.
facts.evidence: 19 U.S.C. § 2411(d)(3)(B)(iii) (Cornell LII, read directly): unreasonable acts include a 'persistent pattern of conduct that— ... (III) permits any form of forced or compulsory labor.' § 2411(d)(3)(C)(i): such acts 'shall not be treated as being unreasonable if the Trade Representative determines that— ... (II) such acts, policies, and practices are not inconsistent with the level of economic development of the foreign country.' USTR's notice instead states its determinations were made 'under sections 301(b) and 304(a) of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 2411(b) and 2414(a))' on the ground that the failure to impose an import prohibition 'is unreasonable and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce.'
facts.explanation: This is the legal hinge of the whole dispute and it is fully checkable from the statute. Congress did put forced labor into Section 301 — but the enumerated clause targets a country's own persistent pattern of permitting forced labor, and it is paired with an express economic-development safe harbor that would plausibly protect several of the poorest economies on the list. USTR's theory is different: not that these countries permit forced labor at home, but that they fail to block imports of forced-labor goods from third countries, which the statute nowhere enumerates. That is not automatically unlawful — the statute says unreasonable acts 'include, but are not limited to' the listed categories, and (d)(3)(A) defines unreasonable broadly as 'otherwise unfair and inequitable.' But it is novel, it sidesteps a safe harbor Congress wrote, and it stretches the separate requirement that the practice 'burdens or restricts United States commerce.' Both sides' strongest legal arguments are in the same paragraph of the same statute.

corroboration.source: USTR — Notice of Determinations, Section 301 forced labor investigations (primary)
CRS — Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs (LSB11460, July 21, 2026)

facts.claim: Whether these tariffs will survive judicial review is unsettled: critics say they are 'unlikely to survive court,' while trade lawyers say Section 301's record makes them harder to strike down than the IEEPA tariffs.
facts.evidence: CRS (July 21, 2026, read directly) identifies four open vulnerabilities without predicting an outcome: whether the conduct is an 'act, policy, or practice' at all; the major questions doctrine's requirement of 'clear congressional authorization' for actions of extraordinary economic significance; APA review of whether USTR's action is 'arbitrary, capricious' or 'unsupported by substantial evidence'; and whether the compressed timeline allowed adequate response to comments. PIIE's Alan Wm. Wolff (July 23, read directly): 'Congress did not delegate authority of such breadth to the president. It cannot constitutionally do so.' Trade lawyer Patrick Childress, quoted in AP coverage (read directly), said these tariffs may be harder to challenge than previous rounds and could persist long-term.
facts.explanation: Graded unverifiable because it is a prediction about litigation that had barely been filed — two suits at the Court of International Trade as of the weekend of July 25-26, with no ruling. The confidence rating here is high in the sense that the state of the question is well established: informed analysts genuinely disagree, and the nonpartisan congressional analysis published three days before the action deliberately declined to forecast. Two asymmetries are worth naming. Section 301 actions are reviewed under the APA, which is more searching than the deferential review given direct presidential action — that cuts toward challengers. But Section 301 comes with a four-month investigative record, hearings and thousands of comments, which is exactly what substantial-evidence review looks for — that cuts toward the government. Anyone asserting certainty in either direction is ahead of the evidence.
facts.source: CRS — Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs to Address Forced Labor and Excess Manufacturing Capacity (LSB11460, July 21, 2026)

corroboration.source: PIIE — Trump's new tariffs over forced labor are unlikely to survive court (July 23, 2026)
Associated Press via Insurance Journal — Trump's New Tariffs Prompt Lawsuit From Small Businesses

facts.claim: The Supreme Court struck down the administration's IEEPA tariffs 6-3 on February 20, 2026, after roughly $165 billion had been collected under that authority, and the administration announced replacement tariffs within hours.
facts.evidence: Holland & Knight client alert (read directly): Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump and Trump v. V.O.S. Selections, Inc., decided February 20, 2026, 6-3, holding that 'IEEPA does not authorize the president to impose tariffs,' with the Court treating tariff authority as 'a branch of the taxing power'; within hours the President announced a 10% global tariff under Section 122 and new Section 301 investigations. Penn Wharton Budget Model (read directly): CBP collected 'approximately $133.5 billion in tariffs under the IEEPA authority' through December 14, 2025 and $164.7 billion by January 2026, with 'up to $175 billion in refunds' projected.
facts.explanation: The decision, date and vote are corroborated by two independent law-firm analyses read directly (Holland & Knight and WilmerHale), which agree on everything but the exact phrasing of the holding — one renders it 'IEEPA does not give the President authority to impose tariffs,' the other 'IEEPA does not authorize the president to impose tariffs.' Confidence is capped at medium for that reason: supremecourt.gov and congress.gov both returned HTTP 403, so the opinion itself could not be opened and the quotation is a paraphrase-level rendering rather than a verified verbatim line. The revenue figures are Penn Wharton's, read directly, and are broadly consistent with the AP's later reference to roughly $166 billion collected. The speed of the replacement — a new authority announced the same day the old one was invalidated — is the fact both sides use, one as diligence and the other as authority-shopping.
facts.source: Holland & Knight — Supreme Court Strikes Down IEEPA Tariffs: What Importers Need to Know Now

corroboration.source: WilmerHale — Supreme Court Strikes Down IEEPA Tariffs — What Now?
Penn Wharton Budget Model — Supreme Court Tariff Ruling: IEEPA Revenue and Potential Refunds

facts.claim: The European Commission publicly welcomed the forced-labor tariffs as consistent with its trade agreement with the United States, while Australia, New Zealand, Japan and Brazil rejected the forced-labor rationale.
facts.evidence: Eunews (July 24, 2026, read directly): European Commission trade spokesperson Olof Gill: 'We welcome the fact that this outcome is in line with the agreed tariff commitments'; the EU rate is 10%, within the negotiated 15% ceiling. Time (July 24, 2026, read directly): New Zealand PM Christopher Luxon: 'Tariffs are not the way — they drive up costs and uncertainty'; Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell called them 'completely unjustified'; Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara called the measure 'regrettable'; Brazil called them 'arbitrary' and 'unjustified.'
facts.explanation: The EU reaction is the single most awkward datum for the human-rights framing: a bloc that USTR formally found had 'failed to effectively enforce' a forced-labor prohibition responded not with denial or reform but by welcoming the tariff as within the ceiling of a previously negotiated trade bargain — which is how governments talk about trade deals, not about sanctions for labor abuses. Confidence is medium rather than high because Reuters, The Guardian and NPR could not be fetched directly (403 / blocked / timeout) and the reaction round-up therefore rests on two readable outlets, Time and Eunews, whose accounts agree with each other and with Fortune's independent report of Brazil's 'arbitrary and unjustified' response. Canada's response is the counterweight and is reported consistently: LeBlanc called the tariffs 'not unexpected' and said Canada maintains 'robust frameworks' against forced labour — a denial of the finding rather than of the rationale.
facts.source: Eunews — New US tariffs: the EU says they're in line with the trade agreement (July 24, 2026)

corroboration.source: Time — How the World Is Reacting to Trump's 'Forced Labor' Tariffs (July 24, 2026)
Fortune — Trump reimposes tariffs on 60 countries using forced-labor law (July 24, 2026)

facts.claim: The tariffs are paid by U.S. importers and largely passed to American buyers; the overall U.S. average tariff rate stands at about 11.1% and is estimated to raise consumer prices by roughly 0.7%.
facts.evidence: Yale Budget Lab, 'State of U.S. Tariffs: July 24, 2026' (page fetched but truncated; figures via two independent secondary reports that agree): 'the shift to new global tariffs results in an effective U.S. tariff rate of 11.1%, which is projected to rise to 11.8% by the end of the year'; consumer price impact of current-law tariff policy estimated at about 0.7%; the rate had reached 13.86% before the February Supreme Court ruling. PIIE (read directly), citing Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers: Americans bear '90 percent of its cost.'
facts.explanation: That tariffs are legally collected from U.S. importers is definitional, and that most of the burden falls on American buyers is the mainstream empirical finding, cited here through PIIE's summary of New York Fed work rather than read in the underlying paper — hence the caveat. Confidence is medium and the verdict is mostly-supported rather than supported for three reasons: the Budget Lab page itself could not be read in full and its figures are taken from two secondary reports that agree with each other but describe the 11.1% as 'effective' in one case and 'statutory' in the other; incidence estimates vary across studies and some pass-through lands on foreign exporters and domestic margins rather than consumers; and the honest counter-fact cuts the other way — the overall tariff rate after this action is *lower* than the 13.86% that preceded the Supreme Court ruling, because the new rates are lower and the exemption list is long. Critics who describe this as an escalation are describing the legal theory, not the average rate.
facts.source: PIIE — Trump's new tariffs over forced labor are unlikely to survive court (July 23, 2026)

corroboration.source: The Budget Lab at Yale — State of U.S. Tariffs: July 24, 2026 [page fetched but truncated; figures via agreeing secondary reports]
IndexBox — U.S. tariff burden lower than at start of 2026 despite new trade measures, Yale Budget Lab finds

facts.claim: Critics including the libertarian-right Cato Institute argue the action is pretextual — that a remedy proportionate to measured forced-labor trade would be under 1%, that the tariffs raise roughly $97 billion a year, and that no published benchmark lets a country earn removal.
facts.evidence: Cato Institute / The Dispatch, Scott Lincicome, July 23, 2026 (read directly): calculations 'suggest warranted tariffs should be 0.23-1 percent, yet proposed rates reach 10-12.5 percent'; the action generates 'approximately $97 billion annually'; the supporting report covers 60 countries in about 80 pages, 'around half a page per country'; there are 'no benchmarks that a country could meet to see the tariffs eliminated'; the piece characterizes the action as 'Trump tariff replacement with a human-rights label glued on top.'
facts.explanation: Graded mixed with low confidence, deliberately. The 'no benchmark' point is checkable and appears to hold: neither USTR's notice, its July 23 release, nor the presidential memorandum publishes criteria by which a country earns removal, and Section 301 actions terminate automatically after four years absent extension (19 U.S.C. § 2417) rather than upon compliance. The proportionality calculation and the $97 billion revenue figure, by contrast, are Cato's own estimates; they were read on Cato's site but not independently reproduced or corroborated by a second analyst, and Cato is an avowed party to the tariff argument. The half-a-page-per-country characterization of USTR's incorporated report could not be verified because the report itself was not obtained. The entry is included because a right-of-center institution making the pretext case is the strongest cross-spectrum corroboration available on this issue — but its arithmetic is presented here as an argument, not as an established figure.
facts.source: Cato Institute — Scott Lincicome, 'Here Comes Another Round of Sham Tariffs' (July 23, 2026)

corroboration.source: CRS — Legal Authority for Section 301 Tariffs (LSB11460): notes criticism of 'cursory factual findings' and automatic four-year termination under 19 U.S.C. § 2417

powerLens.thesis: Two power tests run through this issue, and each party fails one of them. The first is about tariffs themselves. In September 2009 a Democratic president, acting on a petition from the United Steelworkers, imposed 35% safeguard duties on Chinese tires — the first Section 421 relief ever granted, after a Republican predecessor had declined it four times when the ITC found market disruption. Democrats and unions called it enforcement; the free-market right called it protectionism and later priced it at roughly $900,000 per manufacturing job saved. In July 2026 the jerseys are swapped almost perfectly: a Republican president imposes trade restrictions, the Steelworkers and the Machinists applaud, House Ways and Means Republicans call it 'appropriate,' and the sharpest 'this is a sham' essay of the week comes from Cato — while Democratic officeholders and attorneys general argue that tariffs are a regressive tax Congress never authorized. The second test is about executive power and the major questions doctrine. Conservatives built that doctrine to strike down Democratic executive action — the OSHA vaccine mandate, then student-loan cancellation in Biden v. Nebraska, where the 6-3 majority held that 'the basic and consequential tradeoffs inherent in a mass debt cancellation program are ones that Congress would likely have intended for itself,' over Justice Kagan's protest against 'the Court's made-up major questions doctrine.' Three years later the same doctrine is the leading argument against a Republican president's tariffs on 99.4% of imports, it has already cost him one tariff regime 6-3, and the sides have quietly traded scripts: liberals now invoke the made-up doctrine, conservatives now argue that a broadly worded 1974 delegation means what it plainly says. The needle, though, rests on present facts — the statute's text, the rate schedule, the timing, and who pays — not on anyone's consistency.

precedent.case: The September 2009 Section 421 safeguard on Chinese tires — and Biden v. Nebraska's major-questions holding in 2023.
precedent.what: On April 20, 2009 the United Steelworkers petitioned the ITC for relief from Chinese tire imports; on September 11, 2009 President Obama proclaimed additional duties of '35 percent ad valorem above the column 1 general rate of duty' in year one, 30% in year two and 25% in year three, effective September 26. It was the first time a president granted Section 421 relief; President Bush had declined in earlier cases where the ITC found market disruption in four of six investigations. Free-market analysts later estimated the tariff cost $900,000-$925,000 per manufacturing job saved and destroyed roughly three retail jobs per factory job protected. Separately, on June 30, 2023 the Supreme Court held 6-3 in Biden v. Nebraska that student-loan cancellation required clearer congressional authorization than the HEROES Act supplied.
precedent.mirror: Map either precedent onto July 2026 and the roles invert. In 2009 a Democratic administration used a broadly worded trade statute at a union's request and the right called it economically illiterate protectionism; in 2026 a Republican administration uses a broadly worded trade statute, the same union applauds, and the sharpest protectionism critique comes from the libertarian right while Democrats make the consumer-cost argument the right made then. In 2023 conservatives insisted that transformative economic action needs clear congressional authorization; in 2026 the challengers to a Republican president's tariffs make exactly that argument, and the administration's defenders make the capacious-delegation argument that liberals made for the HEROES Act. Neither tribe's stated principle about tariffs or about delegated power has survived the change in who is exercising it.
precedent.source: Obama White House archives — Proclamation to Address Market Disruption from Imports of Certain Passenger Vehicle and Light Truck Tires from China (September 11, 2009)

corroboration.source: CRS — Chinese Tire Imports: Section 421 Safeguards and the WTO (R40844, January 5, 2010)
Cornell LII — Biden v. Nebraska (June 30, 2023)

flips.then: The conservative legal movement spent a decade building the major questions doctrine as a limit on executive action, winning it in the OSHA vaccine-mandate case and in Biden v. Nebraska (2023), where the 6-3 majority reasoned that 'the basic and consequential tradeoffs inherent in a mass debt cancellation program are ones that Congress would likely have intended for itself.' On trade, the party's own recent orthodoxy treated tariffs as taxes on Americans — the critique the American Enterprise Institute made of Obama's tire tariffs, pricing them at roughly $900,000 per job saved.
flips.now: The administration now argues that a 1974 statute's open-ended definition of 'unreasonable' conduct authorizes tariffs on 60 economies covering 99.4% of U.S. imports, having already lost the same fight 6-3 under IEEPA in February — and congressional Republicans who once treated tariffs as taxes now call the action 'appropriate.' The tell is that the strongest 'this is not what the statute means' essay of the week came from Cato, not from a Democrat.
flips.source: AEI — 2009 Tire Tariffs Cost US Consumers $926K per Job Saved (Mark J. Perry, summarizing PIIE research)

flips.then: Democrats spent two decades demanding that trade law be used to enforce labor standards, and a Democratic president delivered the first-ever Section 421 safeguard in 2009 on a United Steelworkers petition, at rates far higher than anything imposed this week — 35% in year one. When the major questions doctrine was turned against a Democratic program in 2023, Justice Kagan's dissent called it 'the Court's made-up major questions doctrine,' and the party treated it as a judicial power grab.
flips.now: Democratic officeholders and attorneys general now oppose a tariff action grounded in labor rights, and the challengers' central argument is the major-questions clear-statement rule the left called made-up three years ago. The awkwardness is on the record and not hypothetical: the United Steelworkers and the Machinists — core Democratic constituencies — publicly praised this administration's action, in USTR's own release, while the party's officeholders denounced it.
flips.source: USTR — American Steelworkers, Manufacturers, and Farmers Praise President Trump's Tariff Action to Combat Forced Labor

powerLens.longRun: Strip out who occupies the White House and one through-line survives: Congress has, over ninety years, delegated so much tariff authority to the executive — Section 232, Section 301, Section 122, Section 421, IEEPA until February — that the only remaining question is which door a president walks through, and the courts have become the sole practical check. That is a structural fact, not a partisan one, and it long predates this administration: every Congress that wrote one of these statutes preferred to hand off a politically painful power rather than exercise it. The predictable sequence when power changes hands is that a Democratic administration will discover the appeal of a broadly worded trade statute for climate or labor conditionality — carbon border adjustments and supply-chain labor rules are already drafted in think tanks on the left — and today's Republicans will rediscover that tariffs are taxes and that agencies need clear congressional authorization. The durable question is the one neither party wants to answer while it holds the pen: whether the tariff power that Article I assigns to Congress should be exercised by Congress. Nothing in the present fight suggests either party will vote to take it back.
powerLens.appliedToScore: The power test docks reasoning-honesty on both sides. The right loses points for arguing for capacious delegation immediately after building the doctrine that says the opposite, and for treating a rate schedule keyed to trade-deal status as a human-rights measure. The left loses points for invoking a clear-statement rule it called judicial invention in 2023, for predicting litigation outcomes that nonpartisan analysis calls genuinely open, and for declining to engage the true predicate — that most of the world has no forced-labor import ban and that its own union allies say so. Neither earns a consistency bonus. But the needle rests on present-tense checkable facts, and those are: does the U.S. ban date to 1930 (yes); do 54 economies lack an equivalent (yes, per USTR's own determinations, uncontested on the merits); does the rate schedule track forced-labor conduct (no — it tracks import-prohibition status and trade-deal commitments, producing the 10%-for-Bangladesh, 12.5%-for-Norway inversion); did the duties begin the hour a different authority lapsed at nearly the same level (yes); did the EU welcome them as consistent with its trade deal (yes); is the legality settled (no). The administration's factual predicate is strong and its calibration claim is weak; the critics have the better checkable case but overclaim on the courts. That is why the needle sits modestly left rather than far left.
powerLens.unknowns: The power test scores consistency of principle, not correctness today. That both parties have flipped on tariffs and on delegation does not make the 2009 tire safeguard and a 99.4%-of-imports tariff wall equivalent in scale, and it does not tell us who is right about what Section 301 means. Whether Democrats would defend an identically structured labor-conditionality tariff imposed by a president of their own party, and whether Republicans would accept a Democratic administration's carbon border adjustment built on the same statutory theory, cannot be known from the present record — though both are worth writing down now.

pattern.thesis: This is not a new tariff policy; it is the third legal vehicle for the same tariff policy in seventeen months, and judging it in isolation is exactly the frame that makes it look like a human-rights measure. The sequence is documented: sweeping IEEPA tariffs from April 2025, struck down 6-3 on February 20, 2026; a 10% global surcharge announced within hours under Section 122, which by statute caps at 15% and dies after 150 days; a 25% Section 301 action against Brazil effective July 22, 2026; the 10-12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariffs on 60 economies effective July 24, timed to the hour of Section 122's expiry; and open Section 301 'excess capacity' investigations aimed at another sixteen economies, which would supply a fourth theory if the third fails. Each step has a defensible statutory rationale read alone. Read in sequence, they describe an administration that has settled on an outcome — a double-digit tariff wall around nearly all imports — and works backward to whichever delegation the courts have not yet closed.

Trump that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, treating the tariff power as a branch of the taxing power reserved to Congress. Customs had collected roughly $165 billion under the authority by January 2026, with refunds projected as high as $175 billion.

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question is not whether Section 301 can reach forced labor — it plainly reaches some labor practices, by Congress's own text — but whether a president may keep the same tariff wall standing indefinitely by rotating the statute underneath it until one survives review. The 'one-off' tell to watch: commentary that argues only about forced labor and never mentions that this tariff replaced an expiring one at the same hour and nearly the same level, or, from the other direction, commentary so busy calling it a sham that it never concedes that 54 economies really do lack a forced-labor import ban and that American unions really do want something done about it. The facts that don't move: the U.S. ban dates to 1930, the rate schedule tracks trade-deal status, the Section 122 clock ran out on July 24, and a fourth theory is already in the pipeline.
pattern.unknowns: The pattern is context that reframes the stakes, not a thumb on the needle, which rests on the day's checkable facts. A sequence of successive statutory theories is consistent with an administration determined to keep a tariff wall by any available authority, and also with an administration pursuing several genuine trade grievances that happen to be actionable under different statutes; the record does not distinguish motive. Whether the excess-capacity investigations will produce tariffs, and whether any court will treat the succession itself as evidence of pretext, is unknowable in July.

notAdjudicable: Whether tariffs are a legitimate instrument of human-rights policy at all — as opposed to sanctions, import bans on specific goods, or diplomacy — is a values judgment about coercion and complicity that evidence about trade flows cannot settle.

Whether higher import prices for American households are worth whatever domestic production and bargaining power they buy is a distributional value choice, not a factual dispute; both the consumer-cost and the industrial-base arguments can be true at once.

Whether pressing lower-income economies to adopt and enforce import prohibitions is solidarity with their workers or an imposition that costs their exporters market access is a genuine moral disagreement, and Section 301's own economic-development safe harbor shows Congress could not settle it either.

Whether Congress should reclaim the tariff power it has delegated across Sections 122, 232, 301 and 421 — knowing that doing so would bind presidents of both parties — is a constitutional-design question about accountability, not a question about who is right this week.

Whether it is better for a president to pursue a contested goal through successive statutory theories until one holds, or to accept the first judicial defeat as settling the matter, is a dispute about the ethics of legal advocacy that no court ruling will resolve.
biasWatch: The bias most clouding this issue is motive-collapse: the assumption that a policy's real purpose is whatever its worst-faith reading suggests, and that establishing the purpose settles the merits. Both sides are doing it in mirror image. Critics reason that because the tariffs replaced an expiring tariff at the same hour, the forced-labor finding must be fake — which does not follow; a pretextual timeline and a true finding can coexist, and 54 economies really do lack an import ban. Defenders reason that because forced labor is real and abhorrent, objections must be motivated by profit or partisanship — which does not follow either; the rate schedule really does track trade deals rather than coercion, and Cato is not a Democratic front. The tell to watch in commentary and in yourself: does the writer ever separate *is the grievance real* from *is this remedy calibrated to it* from *is it lawful*? Those three questions have different answers here — yes, no, and unknown — and anyone who gives you the same answer to all three is running on motive, not evidence. Then apply the swap test, which this issue fails loudly in both directions: if you cheered a Democratic president's 35% tire tariffs granted on a Steelworkers petition, you owe an explanation for treating 10-12.5% duties that the Steelworkers also endorse as self-evidently lawless; if you spent 2023 insisting that transformative economic action requires clear congressional authorization, you owe one for arguing that a 1974 statute's word 'unreasonable' authorizes taxing 99.4% of American imports. And keep what the swap test cannot erase: whoever was president, the rate a country pays would still depend on whether it signed a trade deal rather than on how its workers are treated.
